title: How Snails Work
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Chuck's co-host label in the transcript shown as iHeart Intro) explore snails: their body plan and shell, torsion and the great torsion debate, eyes and senses, mucus, hermaphroditic mating and love darts, eggs and hatchlings, lifespan, ecological roles as recyclers, pollinators and calcium sources, gardener conflicts and invasive species (giant African land snail, rosy wolf snail, common garden snail), snail conservation and extinctions, snails in culture and medicine (escargot, Alzheimer's research, medieval manuscript snail-knight battles), and a listener mail correction about isotopes versus ions.

entities.name: The Strange and Wonderful World of the Snail Wrangler

segments.title: Teaser
segments.summary: Teaser suggesting listeners should appreciate snails after the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with silly banter about a song and introduce the snail topic, which was Josh's pick researched with Allison.

segments.title: Snail research and gastropod classification
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how little academic research exists on snails, malacology, and that snails belong to the class Gastropoda alongside slugs, sea slugs, whelks and limpets.

segments.title: Snail diversity and extinctions
segments.summary: Snails live nearly everywhere and number about 30,000 to 35,000 species out of about 150,000 gastropods. Sizes range from giant African land snails to tiny cave snails. More than 400 snail species extinctions have been recorded, with Hawaii's native snails hit hard.

segments.title: Eating snails and snail caviar
segments.summary: Light banter about escargot served in special plates, and snail eggs sold as white caviar.

segments.title: Snail body misconceptions
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the 'tail' is actually the foot and the head sits inside the shell with the body.

segments.title: Shell, epiphragm and torsion
segments.summary: The epiphragm is a temporary door covering the aperture; the body doubles back through torsion so the head and anus sit near the opening. Fossils cannot show torsion, and gardeners' balance claims are wrong.

segments.title: The great torsion debate
segments.summary: The hosts describe the rotation and asymmetrical hypotheses for why torsion evolved, and say the debate is hard to follow.

segments.title: Radula, eyes and mantle
segments.summary: Snails have a radula, are deaf but can see, with eyes on tentacles that retract. The mantle holds organs and secretes the shell.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Shell growth, breathing and mucus
segments.summary: The shell is calcium carbonate that grows from the outer edge, and snails are born with a starter shell. They breathe through a pneumostome. Mucus from the foot allows climbing, lubrication, moisture retention, and has been used for skin care.

segments.title: Snail trails and mating
segments.summary: Snail mucus trails help snails find each other to mate. Most land snails are hermaphroditic and both can fertilize each other.

segments.title: Courtship and love darts
segments.summary: Snails circle, bite lips and touch tentacles over hours before mating. Love darts form after a first mating and are stabbed into partners, often imprecisely, delivering hormones that protect sperm.

segments.title: Eggs, hatchlings and parental care
segments.summary: Snails can lay up to 450 eggs a year, gestation is 24 hours to about four weeks, hatchlings may eat siblings, and parents may guard young for up to three months.

segments.title: Snail lifespan and snail keepers
segments.summary: Snails live up to five years in the wild and up to 25 in captivity. The hosts discuss the Snail Wrangler documentary.

segments.title: Snails as moisture-loving, decomposers and food web
segments.summary: Snails are called leaky bags of water, need moisture, are mostly nocturnal, eat decaying matter and plants, recycle nutrients, provide calcium to other animals and are part of the food web.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Gardeners versus snails
segments.summary: Burgundy snails eat plants and gardeners dislike them. Hosts advise leaving snails alone and avoiding chemical pesticides.

segments.title: Snail pest control methods
segments.summary: Natural controls include predators like beetles, hand picking at night, and melon or grapefruit traps placed on compost piles. Ferric phosphate and metaldehyde are discussed; metaldehyde is banned in the EU but allowed in the US.

segments.title: Giant African land snail and rat lungworm
segments.summary: The giant African land snail is invasive in Florida, eats many plants and can carry parasites like rat lungworm and cause meningitis. Illegal pet trade spread it to other places.

segments.title: Rosy wolf snail and Hawaii
segments.summary: Rosy wolf snails were introduced in the 1950s to control giant African land snails, and they devastated Hawaii's native snails. Harry G. Lee found 13 snail shells in one rosy wolf snail's gut.

segments.title: Common garden snail as invasive and escargot
segments.summary: Common garden snail is considered invasive in the US after escaping escargot farms. Escargot is the French name for the edible snail.

segments.title: Snail facts: jewelry, Highsmith, Alzheimer's
segments.summary: Snail shells were used as jewelry at least 120,000 years ago. Patricia Highsmith kept snails. Snails are used in Alzheimer's research with pond snails exposed to amyloid beta and snail mucus is being studied as a drug source.

segments.title: Cultural and religious significance, recipes
segments.summary: Giant African land snail is sacred in Yoruba religion. A Nigerian snail recipe called congo meat is mentioned.

segments.title: Medieval manuscript snail battles
segments.summary: Illuminated manuscripts from late 13th-century northern France show knights battling giant snails, possibly comic relief; no one knows the meaning.

segments.title: Listener mail: isotope correction
segments.summary: Listener Nick Lutfi corrects the episode, saying varying neutron number defines isotopes, not electron gain or loss, which defines ions.

segments.title: Mailbag contact and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address and close the show.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Standard show credit.
